# Plans for Next Runs

This documents the creation of the Julia code version 1.3

While all data collected thus far is valid, there are enough difficulties to suggest re-running it all. The *Julia* `MD2` code needs to be upgraded with the following changes.

1.  Make steps a count from the initialization at step zero.\
2.  Remove potential step (count the number of particles interacting and subtract step for PE calculation).
3.  Report the number of particles interacting.
4.  Report stats in correlation calculation.
5.  Add diffusion calculation and report.
6.  Add heating/cooling.

The runs themselves need to be better organized.

a)  Come up with a plan for the distribution of initial energies, taking specific heat calculations into consideration,
b)  Make the run length dependent on energy, so the temperature variance remains the same.
c)  make uniform 4M point runs through the transition region.

## Self Diffusion

The diffusion estimation is given by $\left< r^2 \right>_t = \left< \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^N \left[ \vec{r}_i(t + s) -  \vec{r}_i(s)\right]^2 \right>$

> ...where $N$ is the number of particles, and $s$ is a time used as an initial time. The brackets on the right hand side are meant to indicate an average over different $s$ (typically, 20 different $s$ are used, spaced by 250 steps). $\left< r^2 \right>$ is plotted as a function of time, and then examined to see if the self diffusion is behaving in a linear fashion at long times. If it is, a linear regression is performed on this linear portion. The distinction between linear and nonlinear diffusion is quite obvious and the portion of a configuration showing linear diffusion is easily discerned. The three different results which are likely are shown in Figure 2. It is shown in appendix B that $\frac{d}{d t} \left< r^2 \right> = 4 D$ in two dimensions. [@Shea1980]

In programmatic terms, we will want to parameterize the number of $s$ used, the spacing between the $s$, the number of $t$ estimated, and the spacing between the $t$. The 1980 paper looks as if there were eleven times estimated over a time of about $t = 44 \tau$ so $t_i \approx 4.4 i \tau$. The step size in the 1980 work was not recorded[^1] in the thesis, but was between $0.01768 \tau$ and $0.01786 \tau$, so $44 \tau$ is the equivalent of about 2,476.1 steps. With $s$ spaced at about $4.44 \tau$ and twenty used, that means that $s$ spans about $89 \tau$. Estimating the last $t$ requires data out to about $133 \tau$, or about 7,500 steps in 1980. This is why only four diffusion values were estimated, as 1,000 steps then took about an hour to execute. We'll recast the equation as the following:

[^1]: Memory was that is that $\Delta \tau \approx 0.02 \tau$. The current work was done with a step size of $0.01 \tau$ to ensure proper integration of the equations of motion.

$$
\left< r^2(t_j) \right>_{s_k} = \left< \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^N \left[ \vec{r}_i(t_j + s_k) -  \vec{r}_i(s_k)\right]^2 \right>
$$ {#eq-rsq}

The diffusion calculation requires retention of all particle positions for every $s_k$ and an additional calculation made at each combination of $t_j$ and $s_k$. Of course, the two particle positions in any calculation must be corrected for boundary conditions. We will assume that the distance of any pair or particles will be much less than half the size of space, and we can check that this is so in the calculation.

## Removing potential step

The `rskn` value had to be added to the `rn()` function, which will compute the step and subtract it. This rippled into the testing functions of course, which were upgraded and checked in on 3/2/25.

## Looking at mximum us of `CorrVec.corr`

Getting stats out of `CorrVec()` is not simple. It is a called for every 50 steps, and in a 4M step run it would have 80,000 calls. I didn't want another log file, so I elected to simply record the maximum use of `corr` for every call to `ExecuteSteps!()` and print that value. Also printed the value of `Mmax` used. In the few trials used for testing, `Mmax` was 9,728, but The `maxmt` was only 3,117. This makes sense, as about have of the density would be a unique interaction. Each particle can have, on average, $m=\rho \pi r^2$ particles in the shell, where $\rho$ is the density ($1/\pi$ in the current work) and $r$ is the shell radius (currently 5). A particle at the center of the shell then could be expected to have $m-1$ interactions (since the particle cannot interact with itself). Since each interaction is recorded only once, we might expect $N (m-1)/2$ total interactions (where $N$ is the number of particles, and this number would be 3,072, below what we observed). At higher temperatures, one can imagine local density fluctuations where there are more particles in the shell (if you examine the rest positions, there are 6 particles sitting just outside the shell, for 31). A better `minMmax` might be some small factor above this.

Files were checked in on 3/2/25.

## Speed Testing

Made a simple `BaselineSpeed.jl` script in the `test` directory. It executes a 1,000 step initialization followed by five 5,000 steps executions for each of 13 temperatures, for a total of `13 * 26k = 338k` steps. The following result was obtained

```         
63.401271 seconds (3.89 G allocations: 73.612 GiB, 20.42% gc time, 
50 lock conflicts)
```

64.4s for 78k steps is 0.191s per 1k steps. This is a lot slower than was measured in October of 2025 (0.109s per 1k step), but the condition were different. First, October's data was run from existing files, and we had to initialize today. Second, in October, we saved the data to a solid-state disk. Today, we saved to rotating media, and the 5k step file is almost 1MB in size. This required a small change to `runn()` as it was not handling directories correctly.

This was all precipitated by the realization that `MoveParts!()` squares`tau` for every particle move. Place a `tausq` in `MD2State` so it need only be computed once, and re-ran the speed test. This executed in 57.08 s, so, a bit faster. Files checked in 3/5/25 (Ash Wednesday).

Added several `@inline` and baseline speed ran at 38.71s (0.115s/1k). Actually, added too many (I tried to add the `@inline` to the force and PE functions in `GetForce`, which is ridiculous because they are run-time generated; I had to back these changes out).

## Heating and Cooling

We start with the Verlet algorithm derivation:

$$
x_{n + 1} = x_n + v_n \Delta t + \frac{1}{2} a_n \Delta t^2 \\
\text{where } v_n = \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2 \Delta t}
$$

substituting this into the equation and solving for $x_{n+1}$ a simple result is obtained:

$$
x_{n + 1} = 2 x_n - x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2
$$

If we let the acceleration be velocity dependent such that $\alpha_n = a_n + \beta v_n$ we can derive the following:

\begin{align*}
x_{n + 1} &= x_n + v_n \Delta t + \frac{a_n  + \beta v_n}{2} \Delta t^2\\
   &= x_n + \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2} + 
      \frac{a_n  + \beta \frac{x_{n + 1} - x_{n - 1}}{2 \Delta t}}{2} \Delta t^2\\
   &= x_n + \frac{1}{2} x_{n+1} - \frac{1}{2} x_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}a_n \Delta t^2      + \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n+1} \Delta t - \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t
\end{align*}

This follows:

\begin{align*}      
x_{n + 1} (\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{4}\beta \Delta t) &= 
      x_n - \frac{1}{2} x_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}a_n \Delta t^2 - 
         \frac{1}{4}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t\\
x_{n + 1} (1 - \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t) &= 
      2x_n - x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2 - \frac{1}{2}\beta x_{n-1} \Delta t\\
x_{n + 1} &= 
   \frac{2x_n - \left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t \right)x_{n-1} + a_n \Delta t^2}
            {1 - \frac{1}{2}\beta \Delta t}
\end{align*}

This matches [@Levy1977] result and code, which used `heat1 = 1 / (1 - beta * dt / 2)` and `heat2 = 1 + beta dt / 2` making the update equation `xp1 = (2*xn - heat2 * xnm1 + an dt^2) * heat1`. We'll stuff these in `MD2State` and expose the parameter to `RunSystem()`, the idea being that only one run of heating will ever be executed before many long runs to attain equilibrium (`RunSystem()` will read a `.jld2` file and only make one execution).

While the average acceleration of the particles is zero, the average speed, i.e., $\langle |v_i| \rangle$ is going to be the square root of the temperature ($T=k_B \langle v^2 \rangle$ in two dimensions), and by the above procedure, this will grow by a factor of $\beta \Delta t$ every time step. So, if the temperature (mean kinetic energy) is 0.01, and $\beta = 0.01$ and $\Delta t = 0.01$, then after 1,000 steps, we would expect the average speed to go from 0.1 to \$0.1*(1 + 0.01* 0.01)\^{1,000} = \$ `r 0.1*(1 + 0.01* 0.01)^1000`, and the temperature then to climb to 0.122.

### Runtime dispatch speedtest

The code is currently applying the heating parameters `heat1` & `heat2` for each particle on each step. Generally, that means two multiplies by what amounts to unity. Here is a current timing run. The run script is as follows:

``` julia

@time MD2.newruns( td, tlist, sname, initsteps, steps, runs)
```

## Self Diffusion Computation

We'll remind ourselves of the equation used to estimate self-diffusion (@eq-rsq).

$$
\left< r^2(t_j) \right>_{s_k} = \left< \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^N \left[ \vec{r}_i(t_j + s_k) -  \vec{r}_i(s_k)\right]^2 \right>
$$

The index $i$ covers the particles $N$, the $s_k$ will cover $K$ samples (such that $s_k = s_0 + k\Delta s$), and we will compute the quantity at $M$ instances of $t_j$. While not what we did in 1979, there is now no good reason to let the estimation time ranges overlap. Therefore, $\Delta s > M \Delta t$. The other constraint we'll put on the calculation is to to make $\Delta t$ and $\Delta s$ be multiples of the *Skip* number (the number of steps between calling `CorrShell!()`, currently 50 steps, or $0.5 \tau$). Given our current time step is about half of that used in '79, we'll double the step counts used there.

| Parameter  | Value |     Time |
|:----------:|------:|---------:|
| $t_{max}$  | 5,000 | $50\tau$ |
|    $M$     |    10 |          |
| $\Delta t$ |   500 |  $5\tau$ |
| $\Delta s$ | 5,500 | $55\tau$ |
|    $K$     |    20 |          |

The procedure will be to record the positions of all particles, then execute the $\Delta t$ steps, and then compute $r^2(t_1)$, run $\Delta t$ steps, and so forth until $r^2(t_{max})$ is computed. This will be one of $K$ executions. Once all $K$ estimates have been made, they will be averaged (in R), and the $M$ distance squared estimates reported. There will be $(20 \times 5,000) + (19 \times 500) = 109,500$ steps required. This would have been prohibitive in 1979, as each such estimate would require over 100 hours of computer time, and we need 20 to 30. Today, even on this 7 year old pc (Core i7-7700 \@ 3.60GHz), this will take less than 4 s (after coming to equilibrium, and if run in parallel with other such computations).

110k step runs make for a very long execution, so we will want to break these up into each estimate of $R^(t_j)$ (about 5k steps each). The software works with a call to `RunSystem()`, which can put the diffusion parameters in `MD2State`, and `ExecuteSteps()` will do the work. This will result in one estimate of $R^(t_j)$ (at each of the $t_j$). The entire estimate will be orchestrated by `extendrun()`, which will receive the diffusion parameters $M$, $\Delta t$ (as a multiplier of *Skip*), and $K$. The $\Delta s$ will be implemented by simply one $\Delta t$ worth of steps run before starting the estimates. `extendrun()` is the natural place for this because there must have been equilibrium executions preceding the diffusion estimates. Test runs of twenty 5,000 step executions took about 13s (single diffusion executions cannot be run in parallel).

``` julia
julia> @time "***extendrun diffusion" MD2.extendrun( td, tname * "0030", 7, 
        steps=5000, runs=20, diffFlag=true, Mtau=10, deltat=10, Ks=20)
        
***extendrun diffusion: 12.946641 seconds (5.86 M allocations: 362.085 MiB, 0.36% gc time)
```

We can read in the diffusion data via something like the following (assumes `data.table` is available).

```{r}
require( 'data.table')
dd <- data.table::fread("/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/dev/testdata/Temporary.0030.diff.txt")
str(dd)
```

Each row is an execution (and confusingly, the rows in the above display are the data columns, and vice-versa) and the columns are either three text columns, and then repeating triplets of the time, $\langle D^2 \rangle$, and $\text{max}(D^2)$. That is a clumsy format, although putting an execution number ties too many things in the *Julia* `MD2` code together that would otherwise be independent. The following will unravel the format. Each row is an execution, so we will reshape the table:

```{r}
ddcols <- colnames( dd)
# find column names of the three data types
timecols <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=4, to=length(ddcols), by=3)]
dscols <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=5, to=length(ddcols), by=3)]
dmxcols <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=6, to=length(ddcols), by=3)]
dd[, row := 1:nrow(dd)] # adds row number as last column
ddlong <- reshape( dd, list( timecols, dscols, dmxcols), 
                   v.names=c("Time", "D2", "Dmax"), timevar="group",
                   idvar="row", drop=c("time","d^2", "max d^2"),
                   direction="long")
str(ddlong)
```

The `group` actually groups together the same times, so it is a useless field, but the expression fails if omitted. We can plot the diffusion estimated for each execution by:

```{r}
#| label: PlotDiffusion
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Sample import and plot of diffusion estimates. Each dotted line is an execution, and the solid black line is the average.  The execution number of each line is in the margin. This plot is taken from testdata, and there is no reason to expect the system to be in equilibrium."
# setup the plot window
mxD2 <- max(ddlong$D2) # Find and remember the maximum
plot(NULL, xlim=c(0,50),ylim=c(0.0, mxD2), xlab="Time", ylab=expression(sigma),
     main="Estimate of D^2")
# apply a plot to each row
grid() # add the grid before the lines
invisible( lapply( unique( ddlong$row), 
        function(r) lines( D2 ~ Time, data=ddlong[row == r,], typ="b", col=r,
                           lty=2)))
# plot the means
lines( D2 ~ Time, data=ddlong[, lapply( .SD, mean), by = Time], typ="o", 
       lwd = 2)
ddlast <- ddlong[Time==max(Time), .(row,D2)]
mtext( as.character( ddlast$row), side=4, at=ddlast$D2, cex=0.7, las=1)
```

The maximum diffusion is also important to look at, as it is possible for a particle in a hot system to move far enough to be confused by the periodic boundary conditions, which simply check if the particle distance is more than have the boundary length. While this length is different for the x and y dimensions, the y dimension is the shortest, and is given by

$$
b_x = \sqrt{\frac{N}{2\rho \sqrt{3}}}\\
b_y = \sqrt{3} b_x/2
$$

where $\rho=1/\pi$ is the density, and $N$ is the number of particles (256 in this example), and the dimensions are $\pm b_z$. Therefore, we can write $b_y = \sqrt{\sqrt{3}N\pi/8}$, which is about 13.196. The `Dmax` column is the the maximum of the squared distance, so the maximum distance is `r sqrt(max(ddlong$Dmax))` which is less than the half-y side of `r  sqrt(sqrt(3)*256*pi/8)`, so no particles exceeded that in the estimate.

# Run Errors

Made 71 additional runs on 6 April 2025, but there were steps in the total energy at the execution boundaries.  Here are the results.

``` julia
julia>  td ="/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/Data/1980"
julia> tlist = vcat([i for i in 1:50], [i for i in 52:2:72], [i for i in 75:3:100], [100])
julia> @time MD2.newruns( td, tlist, "S3", 1000, 5000, 6)
julia> @time MD2.newruns( td, tlist, "S3", 1000, 5000, 6)

 80.608085 seconds (131.21 M allocations: 10.197 GiB, 3.50% gc time, 108 lock conflicts)
```

71 runs, each of 31k steps in 80.6s yielding 0.0366s/1k steps. The
`sname` should have been "S3.", so the Unix command
`rename 's/S3(.*)/S3.$1/' S3*` renamed all of the files.

Here was the problem in the TE plots.

```{r}
datadir = "/media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/Data/1980"
xn30 <- combineruns( datadir, "S3", "0030")
plotMD2( as.data.frame( xn30$rundt), dt=0.01)
```

Also at energy `0100`:

```{r}
xn100 <- combineruns( datadir, "S3", "0100", verbose=TRUE)$rundt
plotMD2( as.data.frame( tail( xn100, -1000)), dt=0.01)
```

Examining the files in *LibreOffice Calc* it was apparent that the the first step of each eecution has a small change in the kinetic energy (looked only at `S3.0100.0002.scalars.csv` and `S3.0100.0003.scalars.csv.`, but the discontinuities really look like one at 1,000 steps and regular at 5,000 steps). The source of this must be the change from velocity to `pnm1` (the `*.jld2` files store positions and velocities, but the program propagates the particles using the current {`pn`} and the prior position {`pnm1`} -- when a `.jld2` file is read in the `pnm1` positions are calculated.)

While examining this code, I discovered that the boundary positions are not applied properly. Starting back on 18 July 2024, when the `MoveParts!()` routine was modified to use `FLoops`.  This may have been a typo, but it makes any run after July 18 suspect (at least until this is resolved).  The reversal test was run 11/22/24, and the version checked in the next day (tagged `v1.2`) had the error.

Regardless of this though, there is an error when writing and reading an `MDRecord`, likely due to the translation of the velocity. This requires that the `.jld2` files need to store not the positions and velocities, but the current and the prior positions. This is a rather major change, and will require a reversal test.

Note that the S3 data is considered to be in error and will be deleted (so this document will not be able to be regenerated). The S1 and S2 data likely has the same error, but as a lot of effort was put into its analysis, those files will be retained.
